title: Cognitive remediation to improve the vocational outcomes of people with severe mental illness
source_filename: Cognitive remediation to improve the vocational outcomes of people with severe mental illness.pdf
notes: NOT QUANTIFIABLE. Employment is reported only as the percentage of each randomised group obtaining at least one job: 52.2% (CR+IPS) vs 29.2% (IPS-only) at 8 months and 60.9% vs 37.5% at 1 year (Results, p. 307; Figure 3, p. 307). Table 4 (p. 308) prints mean number of jobs per individual, mean weekly hours worked and mean hourly wage, but no employment count anywhere. Group denominators ARE printed (N=23, N=24), so a numerator could be reconstructed arithmetically; that is back-calculation from a percentage and is prohibited by extraction_v3 rule 1 and codebook rule 2, so the numerator is left blank. The report is in any case outside the primary estimand on three further grounds: employment-related selection at recruitment (previous difficulty maintaining a competitive job AND currently wanting a competitive job), both arms receive an employment-targeted vocational intervention so no whole-cohort row is permissible, and the outcome is cumulative attainment (at least one job during the period), not point prevalence.

title: Effect of individualized occupational therapy on social functioning in patients with schizophrenia: A five-year follow-up of a randomized controlled trial
notes: NOT QUANTIFIABLE. The only work-related measure is the SFS employment/occupation subscale, reported as a group mean on a 0-10 scale (baseline 1.81 SD 2.46 and 1.87 SD 1.96; five-year follow-up 4.46 SD 2.20 and 2.46 SD 2.36; Table 2, p. 482). A subscale mean is not a proportion: no participant is classified as employed or not employed anywhere in the report, so there is no numerator and no denominator to recover. Table 1 (pp. 479-480) reports 'Income, n (% yes)' 96 (94.12%) of 102, but income here is an undefined demographic characteristic covering any source (a 94% rate in a recently hospitalised Japanese inpatient cohort cannot be employment) and it is not offered as an employment outcome.

title: Effectiveness of Antipsychotic Use for Reducing Risk of Work Disability: Results From a Within-Subject Analysis of a Swedish National Cohort of 21,551 Patients With First-Episode Nonaffective Psychosis
notes: NOT QUANTIFIABLE AT ANY FOLLOW-UP TIMEPOINT. Employment is reported only as percentages of the 'main occupational activity' distribution in Figure 1 (p. 942): 32.0% two years before diagnosis, 30.5% one year before, 22.2% in the diagnosis year, then 19.5%, 22.1%, 22.9%, 23.9% and 25.1% at years 1 to 5 after diagnosis. No count is printed for any year and none can be recovered: the figure footnote gives N=21,551 as the base, but that number cannot be the observed denominator at years 1 to 5 (see conflict_note on the result rows). The ONLY recoverable employment count in the whole report is a baseline one: Table 1, p. 941, 'Any income from work during previous calendar year' 7,634 of 21,551 (35.4%). That is a pre-baseline moderator, not a follow-up result, and it is recorded in n_employed_baseline. This is the largest single loss in batch F12: a 21,551-person national register cohort with a printed employment figure at exactly the 12-month landmark and no numerator behind it.

notes: NOT QUANTIFIABLE. The only work-related measure is the PSP subscale 'Social useful activities including study and work', reported as a mean severity-of-problems score on a 0-4 scale where higher scores reflect MORE problems (Table 4, p. 651). No participant is classified as employed or not employed anywhere in the report, so there is no numerator and no denominator. The subscale also conflates paid work with study and with other socially useful activity, so even a count would not have been paid employment. 'Annual income (x 1000)' in Table 1 (p. 649) is a group mean in thousands of euros, not an employment measure.

title: Early recovery and employment outcome 13 years after first episode psychosis
notes: QUANTIFIABLE. Two counts with a common printed denominator at year 13: 67 of 161 with employment income above 100,000 SEK during the year (Table 1 and Results 3.5, p. 378) and 86 of 161 with 'any income' (Results 3.5, p. 378). Neither enters the primary pool. The 67/161 result is threshold-defined (an annual income cut-off) so it is paid_intensity_threshold under D12.3a, not paid_any, and it is a period prevalence over a calendar year, not point prevalence. The 86/161 'any income' figure is never defined: the LISA register as described in this paper carries income from employment, sickness benefits AND student aid, so 'any income' may or may not mean any employment income, and it is coded outcome_construct = unclear pending an author reply. If it does mean any employment income it would be the paid_any numerator for this cohort, which is why it is recorded rather than dropped.

title: Recovery and economy; salary and allowances: a 10-year follow-up of income for persons diagnosed with first-time psychosis
notes: NOT QUANTIFIABLE. Table 3 (p. 923) gives the proportion with income from salary as a percentage only, and only for two post-hoc subgroups: 70% at year 1 and 60% at year 10 in the institutional recovery group (n=53), 53% and 27% in the ongoing institutionalisation group (n=159). No count is printed for any cell. No salary figure of any kind is printed for the 364-person working-age follow-up group, and 152 of those 364 belong to neither reported subgroup and are never described. The subgroups are defined by service contact during the LAST FIVE YEARS of the follow-up, a post-baseline variable strongly associated with the outcome, so even a recovered count would be a selected subgroup and not a whole-cohort prevalence.
